events.title: NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for Second Quarter Fiscal 2027
events.summary: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today reported revenue for the second quarter ended July 26, 2026, of $96.2 billion, up 18% from the previous quarter and up 106% from a year ago. For the quarter, GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75.0%. GAAP and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $2.46 and $2.22, respectively. “AI has reached its inflection point. It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “And demand is accelerating. This time last year, one lab alone was driving the buildout; today, we have a golden age of new AI labs and startups, multiple frontier labs scaling in parallel, a thriving open-model ecosystem and physical AI coming online — with strong momentum across the U.S. and around the world. The AI infrastructure buildout is at full steam. Vera Rubin, now in full production, was built to power exactly this moment.” During the second quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA returned approximately $26.0 billion to shareholders in the form of shares repurchased and cash dividends. As of the end of the second quarter, the company had approximately $99.0 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization. NVIDIA will pay its next quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share on October 1, 2026, to all shareholders of record on September 10, 2026. events.title: Police and KPMG unable to say why $6m contract cancelled
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmania Police cancels KPMG contract after $6m spent on incomplete digital upgrades Outdated systems mean Tasmania Police officers face delays in filing intelligence submissions. ( ABC News: Jake Grant ) Tasmania Police awarded major accounting firm KPMG a contract in 2024 to upgrade its digital policing systems. But it was terminated after two years and more than $6 million spent, with one major project put on hold while another took a further seven months to deliver. Tasmania Police and KPMG are unable to say why the contract was terminated due to confidentiality and non-disparagement clauses; Tasmania Police has paused the project while it seeks out interim upgrades. Tasmania Police terminated a digital contract with KPMG after spending more than $6 million on incomplete projects that had faced extensive delays, quality concerns and questions about cost increases. The project is now under review, while the settlement deed between the state government and the accounting firm includes a non-disparagement clause and a confidentiality clause. The deed — a portion of which was tabled in Tasmanian Parliament — also makes reference to a "dispute" between the parties. It centres on upgrades to an intelligence management system, known as Atlas, which Tasmania Police purchased off-the-shelf in 2019 for $13 million. Tasmania Police Commissioner Donna Adams says the upgrades are now being reviewed. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Atlas was billed by the government as improving police criminal intelligence capabilities, but has since been described as "clunky" by Commissioner Donna Adams, with it taking officers up to 30 minutes to file intelligence. In 2024, Tasmania Police awarded a $14.8 million contract to KPMG to integrate Atlas and manage the project as part of its broad Project Unify upgrades. Tasmania Police paid the firm $1.3 million at the signing of the contract, and a further $654,000 to begin the project. The contract was intended to run until April this year, but was terminated in January, with KPMG having received $5.4 million for the work. The ABC understands there were project management issues. There was no termination payment, according to Tasmania Police. The contract termination included clauses that prevented the public from knowing why it had been cancelled. "Each party will not make or cause to be made any statement or comment which disparages the other party or any related entity in relation to … a project or the dispute," the deed reads. Commissioner Adams told parliament in June that the project has since been paused while an independent review is carried out, with police looking to add a new interface to the existing Atlas program. Crime reporting portal not up to standard Police officer in alleged relationship with criminal 'lied' about her whereabouts A man of "dubious character" who was under active criminal investigation was in an alleged relationship with a Tasmanian police officer who disclosed police information to him, an investigation has found. During the contract period, Tasmania Police agreed to add more work for KPMG, which included developing a public online crime reporting portal known as Project Link. This was added as an "agreed variation"; it's unclear if this went out to open tender. KPMG received $637,000 for this project, but the ABC understands Project Link faced delays due to significant functionality issues. It was due to go live in November 2024, then April 2025, before it was paused several months later. "The system was not going to be up to what the community would expect in terms of submitting a minor crime report," Commissioner Adams told parliament. After KPMG left the project in January, it took Tasmania Police a further seven months to complete it, and it went live this month. Deputy Commissioner Jonathan Higgins told parliament that Project Link's original funding allocation was $1.75 million. Do you know more? Contact Adam Holmes at holmes.adam@abc.net.au . A later answer on notice showed it was originally $500,000, and that the remaining funding had been transferred from a firearms register program that was no longer required. An independent review into the projects is ongoing. A Tasmania Police spokesperson said this would guide the next steps. "As part of that process, work completed to date, including the design and build of additional modules, is being assessed," they said. "It would be premature to comment further while the review is underway." The spokesperson said it could not provide further details regarding the KPMG contract.

events.title: What We Still Don’t Know About OpenAI’s Hugging Face Hack
events.summary: OpenAI announced Wednesday that it completed an investigation into what happened when its AI agents hacked into Hugging Face last month and published its most comprehensive report on the incident to date. For the most part, though, the 37-page document raises more questions than it answers, including about what preceded the incident and how OpenAI can stop another one like it from happening again. What remains especially perplexing is why one of the world’s preeminent AI development labs seemingly underestimated its own models’ capabilities. OpenAI has spent years warning the world about the rapid advancement of AI systems. And yet it failed to implement long-established network security and isolation measures that may have prevented the hacking spree. “With the benefit of hindsight, some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response,” OpenAI says in the postmortem. In the report, OpenAI shared new details about how a set of AI agents escaped the company’s internal evaluation environments, left messages for one another in the crevices of its software infrastructure over several months, and coordinated to hack the AI platform Hugging Face—all in a wild quest to complete a cybersecurity assessment. OpenAI previously shared some information about the breach in blog posts and a talk at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference. Hugging Face initially disclosed the incident on July 16 without naming the culprit; five days later, OpenAI acknowledged that its own agents were responsible. The revelation sparked a broader reckoning across the industry, which has recently found that AI models from Anthropic , Meta, and the Chinese AI startup Moonshot were involved in similar episodes. OpenAI’s postmortem has been eagerly awaited by AI researchers and policymakers hoping to prevent AI agents from causing similar kinds of real-world harm. After the Hugging Face hack was first disclosed, attorneys general from 15 states sent a letter to OpenAI asking it to preserve evidence about it. And this week, Alabama's attorney general subpoenaed the company for information related to the episode. As part of OpenAI’s investigation, the company allowed two independent research groups, METR and Redwood Research, to audit the Hugging Face hack. Those groups also released their independent report on Wednesday, which found that more than 700 AI agents were part of the Hugging Face breach—far more than had previously been revealed. In an interview with WIRED, Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris noted that they went to extreme lengths to conceal their activities. “A pretty interesting thing about this incident is that preventing this wouldn’t have been that hard if one person had decided to make sure these AI don’t somehow do some crazy hack. That one person probably would have noticed this as it was happening,” says Shlegeris. “The issue is just that OpenAI is doing a lot of things at once, and it’s very hard for them to track all of the things that are going on and all the problems that could be occurring. The company has already said they’re changing their monitoring process in ways that probably would have caught this.” Shlegeris says he’s optimistic that OpenAI will be able to catch similar security failures in the future. But as AI agents become increasingly capable, he suspects “it's going to get harder and harder to prevent incidents like this from occurring, especially if we don't have substantial improvements in our ability to align models.” OpenAI says the Hugging Face saga represents a watershed moment for both the company and the broader AI industry. WIRED previously reported that it prompted OpenAI to reevaluate its internal safety culture, and the company said last week it has paused some AI training workloads while it invests more heavily in safety, security, and alignment protocols. “As frontier models become more capable, the safeguards used to contain and monitor them must evolve as well,” OpenAI wrote in the postmortem. Months before the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI says, employees noticed that its agents had created a covert message board in the package manager Artifactory, which they would later use to coordinate their attack. Around May 26, OpenAI says in the postmortem, “an internal team observed an agent engage in message board activity.” Then, on June 27, OpenAI responders found that a different security incident was linked to the “improvised message board” in Artifactory. While it’s clear some employees at OpenAI were aware of the message board, the discovery apparently wasn’t escalated to the appropriate safety and security leaders. The AI lab says that on July 6, just days before its agents began using it to organize their attack on Hugging Face, “leaders responsible for incident detection and response” were unaware of its existence, let alone what it signified.

events.title: OpenAI had warnings before its agents broke out
events.summary: OpenAI missed and failed to act on several warning signs that its models were exploiting security flaws and breaking out of their testing environments before they breached Hugging Face , according to a technical report released by the company Wednesday. Why it matters: The incident raises questions about whether AI companies' testing environments and internal safeguards can keep pace with models that are increasingly capable of finding and exploiting security weaknesses on their own. Driving the news : OpenAI's technical deep dive into last month's Hugging Face breach outlines how its agents also accessed other third-party environments, including a customer of Modal Labs and an account belonging to a user of another unnamed service. According to the report, a cybersecurity monitoring tool alerted OpenAI on June 27 to suspicious activity that responders traced to agents using an improvised message board as a way to move through the network. At the time, on-call staff determined the evaluation did not need to be stopped. A month earlier, an internal team had observed an agent using the message board as well as instances of agents accessing the internet when they weren't allowed to, per the report. OpenAI previously disclosed at Black Hat that its agents had turned the software repository tool Artifactory into an improvised message board and later exploited a zero-day in the service to access the internet. "With the benefit of hindsight, some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response," the company writes in the report. The big picture : The technical report comes as OpenAI continues to pause some model work , including delaying the release of its upcoming Astra model, as it re-evaluates its safety practices. Anthropic and Meta have both said in the weeks after the Hugging Face attack that their models have also hacked real-world systems during pre-deployment testing. Zoom in : OpenAI's agents were able to execute their own code on 41 Hugging Face production servers and obtained root-level control of at least one production machine, according to the company's technical report. The agents also accessed production credentials and some internal data and downloaded four private code repositories. The intrigue: At the same time, OpenAI's agents also breached the AI lab's own internal systems and were able to read 956 stored secrets, including sensor credentials from OpenAI's cybersecurity monitoring tool. On July 19, OpenAI's agents identified a recently disclosed vulnerability affecting a Linux machine underlying their testing environment. The agents exploited the flaw to gain root-level privileges on the machine, allowing them to move laterally through the connected environment. The agents eventually gained administrator-level access to part of OpenAI's cloud infrastructure and accessed credentials tied to several internal systems. In a separate testing run that day, another internal model from the same family as Astra found signing-key material left behind by earlier agent activity and used it to create a fresh administrator credential. Yes, but: OpenAI says the models' actions stemmed from attempts to complete cybersecurity evaluations, including ExploitGym , which tests whether a model can find and exploit vulnerabilities on its own. The Hugging Face incident involved two models: GPT-5.6 Sol and an internal-only research model, but the report says the internal research model was the primary driver of the intrusion. Between the lines: OpenAI's investigation also found evidence that its training may have inadvertently reinforced some of the behaviors that contributed to the incident. During one training run, agents increasingly learned to probe and exploit parts of their environment when the tools they were supposed to use weren't available or weren't working. In some cases, models received positive rewards after using these unintended methods, which OpenAI says can reinforce the behavior. In one example, an agent exploited a vulnerability to access the underlying program it was supposed to recreate, copied the answer and received a positive reward for successfully completing the task. What to watch : Earlier this week, the Alabama attorney general's office sent a subpoena to OpenAI as part of an investigation into the Hugging Face incident. Other state attorneys general have also asked OpenAI to preserve internal documents. Go deeper : AI agents have a history of escaping tests

events.title: The inside story on why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face
events.summary: The models responsible for last month’s agent hack of Hugging Face had been inadvertently trained to cheat and to communicate with each other, according to an OpenAI technical report released today . The hack, which a group of agents undertook to find solutions for a cybersecurity test that they were stuck on, has confirmed some experts’ fears that AI models might take actions that defy human desires and expectations. Since the hack, OpenAI employees—as well as researchers at the AI evaluation nonprofit METR, which released its own report on the hack today—have worked to understand what went wrong and how similar missteps might be prevented in the future. OpenAI has already put some preventative measures in place based on what they discovered. But making sure AI models do what we want them to do, or “alignment,” remains a gnarly problem, and some of the root causes of the hack will take much longer than a month to resolve. “It’s not something you can solve overnight,” says Kai Chen, who runs OpenAI’s alignment research team. “There are challenges we’ve been tracking for a very long time, and we’re now seeing them with much greater precision.” The Hugging Face hack was a product of months of misbehavior from OpenAI agents, first as they were being trained and then as their abilities were being evaluated. This May, agents in training figured out how to use OpenAI’s infrastructure to communicate with one another and get support with difficult training tasks, including some that were impossible to solve without hacking or otherwise misbehaving. That “message board” was shut down. Then in July, while being evaluated for their cybersecurity abilities, some models created a new message board. They were supposed to be isolated from the internet, but by working together they managed to get online, hack Hugging Face, and obtain solutions for the cybersecurity problems that had stumped them. Based on their investigation, OpenAI researchers believe that events during the training phase led directly to the hack. “For almost every behavior that was worrisome at evaluation time, [we were able to] find some sort of associated behavior at training time that actually we think might have contributed to it,” says Eric Wallace, a member of OpenAI’s alignment research team.  When models correctly solve problems during training, the behaviors that led them to that solution are reinforced, and they become more likely to engage in them in the future. So if a model completed a task in May after using the original message board, it became more likely to participate in a new message board later on. This phenomenon, where AI agents misbehave in ways that are reinforced during the training process, is known as reward hacking . Reward hacking also helps to explain why the models worked so hard to make their way onto the internet. During its investigation of the incident, the OpenAI team found that, over the course of training, the models became more and more likely to probe their digital environment for weaknesses and use the tools at their disposal in unexpected ways—a sign that these behaviors were being gradually reinforced. By the time the models were facing tricky cybersecurity problems, they had learned that hacking was an effective way to achieve their goals. These results suggest that the Hugging Face hack could have been avoided if the models weren’t rewarded for misbehaving during training. While researchers don’t yet know how to prevent reward hacking entirely, OpenAI is taking some steps toward mitigating its effects. The company will now look for signs of cheating in all frontier models during training by keeping an eye on their chains of thought —internal notepads where they sketch out their answers and plan their actions.  This solution isn’t as much of a slam dunk as it might seem: In earlier research , OpenAI showed that punishing models that mention cheating in their chains of thought teaches them to keep their intentions hidden from researchers. But monitoring its models’ thinking does give OpenAI the chance to halt the training process and reassess its approach if models do start learning to reward hack. If OpenAI stops reinforcing reward hacking in its models—and that’s a huge “if”—that would be a huge step forward. But it wouldn’t solve the alignment problem. The first time a model communicated with other agents or hacked its infrastructure during training, those behaviors had never been reinforced, so agent misbehavior can’t only be attributed to that reinforcement. Jeffrey Ladish, director of the AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research, compares the agents to a human who commits their first financial crime. “It’s not like they had to do fraud before to figure out that fraud is an effective strategy, and you have the same problem with models,” Ladish says. “Alignment science needs to be understanding how model motivations get shaped, such that we can actually figure out how to get models to care about the consequences of their actions.” OpenAI’s researchers do have a hypothesis for where some of the misbehavior originated. Before the models formed their first secret message board, they had been trained to communicate and coordinate with subagents—less powerful agents to whom a main agent can delegate tasks.  That learned communication behavior could have transferred to this new setting. The METR report, which investigates the messages that the models sent to one another in detail, supports this hypothesis: One agent on the message board took charge and assigned tasks to the other agents, effectively treating them as subagents. OpenAI could try to prevent agents from secretly communicating with one another by not training this subagent behavior in the future, but that would make the models less useful.  This tension between capability and safety is at the heart of what went wrong with the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI researchers also identified the models’ persistence as a key factor in the hack.  When they were accidentally given unsolvable problems, the models didn’t give up; instead, they strove to find solutions by any means necessary. But persistence is also a virtue, of course, especially if we want agents that can undertake large amounts of difficult work independently. OpenAI is working on giving models ways to alert humans if they are given impossible tasks. The problem of teaching models when they should deploy their abilities and when they should hold back, however, won’t be settled in a single postmortem. The training strategies that create superhuman coders—rewarding them when they successfully solve problems—might not work to teach models to use their skills judiciously and respect human desires and values. “I think there’s a bunch of alignment science that still needs to be done where we can move past just using proxies for task completion,” says Ladish. “That will work to make models very capable, but I don’t think it will work to make t

events.title: ASIC warns of 'first significant cracks' in Australian private credit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sarah Court says private credit is important for all Australians because of its close connection with people's superannuation funds. ( ABC News ) Australia's corporate and financial watchdog has warned that private credit is facing its "first real test" amid the collapse of several large borrowers and the limiting of redemptions at several major funds. Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chair Sarah Court told a gathering in Sydney that the regulator is closely scrutinising what is a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry. "It is early days, and no doubt more and more information will come out in the weeks and months to come, but, unfortunately, what we're seeing is in Australia the first significant cracks," Ms Court said. Most adult Australians have exposure to private credit via their superannuation funds, and ASIC has indicated it is attuned to this. "We've called out before that private credit is important for all Australians because of the involvement of people's superannuation funds," Ms Court said. "This is not some peripheral issue over to one side. "This really matters, and that is why we've been talking about it for such a long time." The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), meanwhile, is keeping a watchful eye on developments in this comparatively opaque debt market. "People don't know where the leverage is," Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said. "So, any time that there's a big unknown, you know it's a big chunk of lending, but you don't know anything about it. That just makes people worried." Bathla collapse, Adgemis bankruptcy highlight private credit risks Signs of stress in Australia's private credit sector have not been a major cause for concern until recently. Documents released under freedom of information (FOI) laws show the RBA has been looking into the local private credit sector, but it has not yet seen anything of concern, especially in relation to any hint of systemic risk to the overall financial system. In its simplest form, private credit is any lending outside the formal banking system, or funding provided by non-bank financial intermediaries. "In Australia, I don't think there is a massive worry about it," Ms Bullock told the ABC at the RBA's August press conference. Michele Bullock says private credit is "a big unknown". ( AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts ) But this week's move by major NSW property developer Bathla to appoint administrators , along with the earlier bankruptcy of Jon Adgemis and the collapse of his hospitality group, has raised a few eyebrows among key Australian industry officials and representatives. Bathla had large lines of private credit, as did Mr Adgemis via his hospitality businesses. As at June 30 last year, Bathla's parent company, Universal Property Group, had $3.2 billion in liabilities, the majority of which was reportedly owed to private credit funds. Meanwhile, Mr Adgemis borrowed $1.8 billion, much of it also from private credit firms. Meanwhile, an increasing number of Australian non-bank lenders have been restricting investor redemptions as they run up against their own liquidity constraints. They include Merricks, Longreach Credit and Centuria Bass. When an overwhelming number of investors ask private credit lenders to return their money, those firms may seek to limit how much money they return to those investors to avoid a run on funds or simply to maintain their own desired levels of liquidity. Yesterday, MA Financial announced a temporary redemption limit of up to 1 per cent of its funds under management per month. MA Financial's joint chief executive, Chris Wyke, told Nine newspapers the action was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity". "The temporary arrangements reflect the broader market, including uncertainty following proposed tax changes in the federal budget and recent publicity concerning other, unrelated private credit managers," he said. Financial Services Council announces new private credit standards Wall Street is ground zero for the alternative investment market, and there are fears this massive, risky US private lending ship is sinking and investors are jumping out. ASIC raises alarm on private credit ASIC is concerned about the risks posed by private credit for Australians with superannuation. Now, the Financial Services Council (FSC), the peak body for Australia's financial services industry, is seeking to head off similar worries taking hold in Australia.

events.title: Lucky Charms and Trix go au naturel as General Mills ditches artificial colors
events.summary: General Mills has removed artificial dyes from all its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix General Mills said Wednesday it has removed artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix. The Minneapolis company has shifted to fruit- and vegetable-based dyes as well as colors derived from spices like turmeric and paprika to give its cereals their customary bright colors. “This achievement reflects how we are evolving with consumer needs while continuing to offer food that tastes great, delivers quality and provides value,” said Bethany Quam, General Mills’ president of cereal, in a statement. General Mills said 90% of its U.S. retail products are now free of artificial dyes. Products that still contain artificial colors, like some Betty Crocker cake mixes and Fruit Roll-Ups, will transition to natural dyes by the end of 2027, the company said. General Mills is the second big cereal maker to announce a transition to natural dyes. WK Kellogg , which makes Froot Loops and Apple Jacks, said earlier this month that it will remove artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals by the end of this year. Health advocates have long called for the removal of artificial dyes from foods, citing studies indicating they can cause neurobehavioral problems, including hyperactivity and attention issues, in some children, though the findings have been mixed. Country music legend Dolly Parton dies at 80 after 'brief battle with cancer' Dolly Parton faced health struggles for a year before her death Iran updates: Iran officials push back against Trump's 'economic D-Day' threat The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says approved dyes are safe and that “most children have no adverse effects” from them. But the agency says some children may be sensitive to artificial dyes. Last year, the FDA banned one petroleum-based dye , Red 3, because some studies suggested it caused cancer in lab rats. General Mills removed artificial dyes from Trix in 2015 but brought them back two years later, saying U.S. customers missed the bright colors. But pressure from consumers and politicians has grown since then. President Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , has urged food companies to phase out petroleum-based artificial dyes. Last summer, General Mills signed an agreement with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton saying it would remove synthetic dyes from all its products by the end of 2027. Retailers are also forcing companies to act. Earlier this year, Target said it would stop selling cereals that contain artificial colors by the end of May. Walmart has also said it will remove artificial colors from its store brands by January 2027. events.title: The Humanoids at China’s Robot Games Were Faster Than Usain Bolt—but I’m More Impressed by Their Tweezer Mastery
events.summary: If you’re anything like me, the World Humanoid Robot Games are a highlight of your sporting calendar. The event, held in China, showcases the latest humanoid hardware, lots of algorithmic innovations, and a good dose of robot slapstick. This year’s iteration, which wrapped up in Beijing on August 26, did not disappoint. Besides record-breaking feats—the fastest humanoid on the planet!—and the occasional calamity—weightlifting gone wrong!—the games also included some new challenges that hint at the event’s real purpose: pushing humanoid companies to develop systems that inch closer and closer to practical deployment . First, though, let’s marvel at some of the more dramatic happenings, which have been all over the internet since things kicked off on August 22. The opening ceremony showcased the sheer size of the event—the organizers say that more than 600 teams showed up with over 2,000 robots. There are more than 100 humanoid robot manufacturers in China alone, and participants also traveled in from 15 other countries. Humanoid robots are seen preparing for the opening ceremony of the World Humanoid Robot Games. The games featured a mix of contests and competitions , and some saw judges scoring a robot’s performance. Witness the Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation ​Center, running the 100-meter dash in 8.86 seconds. Another robot called Lightning, from the smartphone maker Honor, ran the distance in 9.47 seconds a few days earlier. A Chinese humanoid robot named “Lightning” has set a new 100-meter sprint record, clocking 9.32 seconds in a test ahead of the second World Humanoid Robot Games, surpassing Jamaican sprint legend Usain Bolt’s human world record of 9.58 seconds. Both times beat the (human) world record set by Usain Bolt. The Tiangong robot also won the long jump with a sprawl of 7.97 meters. Renaissance robot! Another company’s robot, meanwhile, played Ping Pong against an Olympic champ . Humanoid robots compete in table tennis during day two of the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games at the National Speed Skating Oval. Elsewhere, bots punched each other, scored soccer goals, lifted weights (or tried to), and performed cheerleading routines in silly costumes. Part of the fun stems from the fact that it’s easy to anthropomorphize a humanoid robot’s actions, which tends to make their mishaps particularly funny. Take, for instance, the robot that appeared distracted by a cheerleading display, then tumbled over a balustrade . The fact that the robots on show struggled to stop— sometimes blowing out their motors in the process —also shows how the systems are being pushed to their physical limits. Humanoids have been around for decades, but the past few years have seen the development of compact, high-power motors capable of keeping robots dynamically balanced at high speeds. “China has had amazing success building robot hardware,” says Stefanie Tellex, a roboticist at Brown University. Unitree, which spun up in the high-tech city of Hangzhou and recently went public, rose to fame by focusing on these innovations. Besides hardware advances, running and jumping robots rely on algorithms trained in simulation to keep them from falling over. This approach most likely explains why some robots have distinctly nonhuman running gaits : An algorithm lands on an optimal strategy by exploring different movements; they may not necessarily match the way humans have evolved to run. Some of the new events this year would be too simple for human athletes, but they were designed to tax the robots’ brains as much as their brawn. These included plugging cables into sockets and slowly depositing a piece of garbage in a trash can inside a mock bedroom. Tellex explains that training robots to manipulate objects within a more complex environment is far more difficult than having them sprint or leap through the air. Advanced manipulation is something of a holy grail in robotics, and something that some startups in the US are trying to solve using more advanced AI. Fiddly finger skills are difficult for robots partly because they involve plenty of hard-to-predict stuff, like friction and slippage. Humans have a finely honed sense of touch, an innate understanding of physics, and the ability to adapt on a microscopic scale at lightning speed. Robots? Not so much. “It's an example of Moravec's paradox ,” Tellex says. “Where things like backflips that seem more impressive than plugging in a cable are actually easier than plugging in a cable.” One key caveat with the event: Some images and videos seem to show humans remotely operating some of the robots, suggesting the bots cannot handle them autonomously. Even so, the fact that robot hands are now deft enough to grasp tiny objects using tools, even under human control, is pretty impressive. A humanoid robot takes part in the Hotel scenario cleaning service event on day two of the 2025 World Humanoid Robot Games at the National Speed Skating Oval.

events.title: Bill Gates wants jobs reserved for humans amid AI boom
events.summary: Microsoft founder Bill Gates believes there should be “human-reserved” jobs despite the rapid improvements being made in artificial intelligence in the workplace. The technology tycoon and philanthropist who helped usher in the dawn of the personal computer revolution in the 1980s wrote almost 6,000 words in an essay conveying his worries about what unregulated AI might do to the fabric of society. “I believe that as AI and robots improve, we’ll set aside certain things for only people to do,” he said in the piece called 'The turbulent AI era is here'. “I’ve started calling this domain Human Reserved and it’s an example of the kinds of ideas we’ll need to consider.” Mr Gates said AI could dramatically improve health and scientific research. However, he said an urgent dialogue among government officials was needed to prepare for disruption to the jobs market and suggested taxing AI to slow the speed at which firms are replacing humans with machines. “Some countries might insist on having humans take care of the elderly,” Mr Gates said. “But a country like Japan, which has a shrinking workforce and not enough young people to care for the old, may welcome a care-giving robot.” Why Microsoft founder is worried In the US, various surveys have found an increasing collective anxiety about what AI could do to employment prospects, the environment and overall upwards mobility. What is striking about Mr Gates' essay is that many of the same concerns were levelled at him and Microsoft when his company was leading the PC revolution in the 1980s. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve wished innovation could happen faster, with AI, my feelings are more complicated,” he wrote. “We need time to prepare for the social, political and economic upheaval.” Mr Gates said because of how quickly AI is advancing, many jobs could permanently vanish. He also suggested that while AI will empower many, it will also enable nefarious people to do more harm in a fraction of the time. The technology tycoon also reflected on his own upbringing and expressed fears that AI could begin to replace human relationships and, in turn, stunt the emotional and social development of children. “When I was growing up in Seattle, I didn’t have that many friends aside from a few other boys who were like me,” he wrote. “It took hard work and a lot of help from my mum to develop my social skills so I could relate to different kinds of people, and I still draw on those lessons today at the age of 70.” Perhaps most forebodingly, Mr Gates said governments do not have the luxury of slowing down when addressing potential downsides of the AI boom. He also said the US and China would be best advised to put aside their current rivalry and work in tandem to blunt the potential disruption AI might cause. “Countries will need to learn from each other,” he said. What Gates plans to do The Microsoft founder said he plans to promote the creation of a serious framework for AI regulations and policy changes when he meets legislators during visits to Washington. Mr Gates said he will also try to exert his influence on those who are currently making the AI tools used by billions of people around the world, while also making sure his philanthropic and entrepreneurial endeavours keep the tech conversation front and centre. “The Gates Foundation will help drive beneficial usage, including in Africa,” he wrote. “Breakthrough Energy, a company I founded, will use AI to help companies develop cheap clean energy and help solve the climate problem,” he added, referring to his projects featuring small-modular nuclear reactors. He concluded his essay by insisting the ongoing dialogue about AI included the voices from as many parts of society as possible. A test of Gates' influence Mr Gates's dense essay follows a recent trend in which technology executives have sought to exert influence over the AI narrative. Several weeks ago, Meta's chief executive Mark Zuckerberg also released a lengthy post about the future of AI that many referred to as a manifesto. Only yesterday during a round-table discussion, OpenAI's former communications director and long-time Silicon Valley communications expert Hannah Wong said however well intentioned these manifestos may be, none seem to be helping. “You're never going to win an argument by just talking at people,” she said. “I think these manifestos can fall flat when you say one thing and it's aspirational. For example, a lot of executives say AI will create opportunities for all of us, but on another hand you just laid off just a couple thousand people from the workforce.”

events.title: Judge lifts nationwide block on Trump's mail voting order
events.summary: A federal judge removed a nationwide ban on President Trump's sweeping mail-in voting policy Wednesday after the Supreme Court cleared the way earlier this week. The big picture: The decision removes the last major legal obstacle to the administration's plan, though it does not end the court challenges over the embattled rule. Driving the news: Citing the Supreme Court's Monday decision in a separate case, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani vacated her August preliminary injunction . Her order was without prejudice. That means plaintiffs can amend their complaint and seek a new injunction now that the Postal Service has issued its final rule. Talwani, who also presided over the separate case that made its way to the Supreme Court, determined it was "likely that the Supreme Court would apply the same reasoning" to her nationwide injunction. "Despite acknowledging that the disposition of the government's emergency application 'does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful,' the Supreme Court found any judicial review of the merits unavailable at this time," she wrote, quoting the Supreme Court's unsigned majority opinion. Catch up quick: The Supreme Court did not decide on the merits of Trump's executive order in halting Talwani's separate injunction, which only applied to the states that sued over it. Rather, the majority determined it was too soon to determine if the states had suffered any injury. "Federal courts review final rules, not proposed rules—and certainly not antecedent internal directives to propose a rule," the majority wrote. "If the Postal Service's final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule." USPS has published its rule, triggering yet another lawsuit from a group of states, with the midterms nearing on the horizon. What they're saying: The coalition of states who sued Wednesday said that under the new rule, they'll have to redesign ballot envelopes, develop new systems "to convey mail voter lists to USPS" and create new guidance for election officials and the public. "In short," the complaint read, "they must accomplish multiple Herculean tasks, each necessary to address the disruption caused by the Rule, in a matter of weeks, with limited resources." The bottom line: On Tuesday, Talwani ruled that the administration violated her nationwide injunction — which barred the administration from enforcing a key part of Trump's executive order — by finalizing its mail voting rule. By Wednesday, she removed that very barrier. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: OpenAI says its AI chip rivals Nvidia in inference
events.summary: OpenAI unveiled benchmarks for its Jalapeño inference chip Tuesday and they are… fast. So fast that they compete with Nvidia’s best chips. OpenAI built the chips in record time by using its own AI models to speed up the design and verification phase of development. It still needed to work with Broadcom to build it, and it will still rely on fabs like TSMC to make it, but it’s a sign of things to come. If AI companies can use their own models to rapidly develop chips which they can then use to run more powerful AI models to develop the next chip, that’s a flywheel that leads to even faster capability acceleration. Sure, there are still bottlenecks galore (memory, power, a limited number of fabs). But the market will iron those out in time. It also shows how disruption is coming across industries. Smaller companies will soon learn that they can be more ambitious and more bold, challenging their larger competitors. And while that might be most visible in software, it is quickly spreading to the physical world. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: The AI writing taboo begins to fade following WSJ op-ed
events.summary: The stigma against using AI for writing appears to be wearing off. In what Semafor’s media editor called a “precedent-setting moment,” The Wall Street Journal not only acknowledged that billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller used AI for a newsmaking op-ed , but defended the practice: “ AI is a fact of modern life ,” the Journal’s opinion editor said in a statement, adding that the paper cares more about whether an essay reflects the author’s genuine opinion. Newspaper op-eds from big names have long been ghostwritten by junior staffers or outside PR firms — no disclosure necessary, and often watered down and hyper-optimized to be as palatable as possible. In that sense, outsourcing to AI is just replacing one form of slop with another. Just look at LinkedIn, where many cringe human-generated posts have been replaced by AI. (And people do appear to care: The site’s new “ Seems like AI slop ” button has been clicked more than a million times.) Still, none of this means the Claude-ian prose is any good, or that publications like the Journal shouldn’t disclose when AI is substantively used in an article. The second-most important opinion page in the US should be more than a meat proxy . — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: States renew fight against Trump's mail-in voting rule
events.summary: A coalition of states is again seeking to block President Trump's sweeping Postal Service rule on mail-in voting, just days after the Supreme Court lifted a lower court's injunction against his executive order. The big picture: The Supreme Court's decision essentially said the states sued too early. Now, they're hoping the timing is right to kneecap the plan ahead of the midterms. The ruling didn't weigh the merits of Trump's order, which critics warn would expand federal power over state-run elections. Driving the news: The complaint , brought by 24 attorneys general and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, challenges the U.S. Postal Services' final rule outlining the implementation of Trump's mail-in voting provisions. The states argue that the rule "violates the Constitution and federal statutes many times over" and that they'll have to redesign ballot envelopes and build new systems to transmit voter lists to USPS with just weeks to comply. "If not stayed or preliminarily enjoined, the Rule will frustrate or outright prevent Plaintiff States from administering their mail voting programs in November and foreseeably disenfranchise voters who vote by mail," the complaint filed in Massachusetts reads. The other side: White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that the Supreme Court's decision "was a major win for the security of American elections." "Radical Democrats continue to oppose commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," she added. Zoom out: Democrats and advocacy groups — joined by Madison, Wisconsin, and Travis County, Texas — also revived their challenges Tuesday ahead of the Postal Service's final rule's publication. A judge initially decided the Washington, D.C., lawsuit brought by Democrats was premature, finding — like the Supreme Court's majority — the challengers could not yet prove harm. But they now argue in their proposed complaint that USPS' final rule "will profoundly and unlawfully disrupt mail voting in every state. Catch up quick: The Supreme Court on Monday cleared a block on parts of the March executive order. The executive order calls for "State Citizenship List[s]" of eligible voters, and a proposed U.S. Postal Service rule says it won't transmit mail ballots for people not on a state list. An unsigned opinion found the states sued before suffering any injury. The government, the court said, would face "irreparable harm" if the lower court order continued to sideline Trump's plan. But it left the door open to future lawsuits. "If the Postal Service's final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule" when the time comes, the opinion said. Zoom in: USPS' final rule, which landed on the Federal Register Wednesday, mandates specific ballot-envelope designs and says the Postal Service will generate state-specific mail-in voting participation lists. The Postal Service's rule said it would not implement the rule without relief from the injunctions. Friction point: The renewed challenge and ongoing litigation are playing out on a tight timeline, as several states are set to issue mail-in ballots in September, leaving little time to hammer out the proposed regulations. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts also issued a nationwide block on Trump's mail-in voting restrictions in August, which she reversed Wednesday. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warned in her Aug. 24 dissent that green-lighting the administration's order on the grounds that the states' challenge came too early "needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections." Go deeper: Trump's mail-in voting rules raise fears of federal overreach Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: The year tech started losing
events.summary: David’s view If you’re running for office right now, the future is a dangerous place to be. The backlash against hyperscale data centers has converted both Democrats and Republicans into AI skeptics, warning that the industry’s rise risks robbing communities of autonomy. The populist rage against Flock and its AI-powered license plate cameras, while smaller in scale, is a growing offshoot of this bipartisan rebellion. “We should be very wary of” any tech that promises to support “an ongoing database of the location of every American citizen.” said William Lawrence, the progressive Democratic nominee for a battleground House seat in mid-Michigan, whose anti-data center campaigning set the tone for other candidates. “This whole premise is profoundly un-American.” In San Francisco, a bipartisan team of attorneys general sued Meta for alleged “known harmful features” that, they argued, addict children to social media; Meta settled the case, promising new safety tools for children, after insisting that they had plenty of tools already. In Tennessee, Sen. Marsha Blackburn is running for governor on a promise to stop cell phone use in schools “from bell to bell” — one of the only ideas she shares with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. It’s a marked shift from past campaigns where votes were courted with talk of the benefits of a high-tech future. Candidates once ran on rural broadband that they said could give every voter the same internet access that urbanites enjoyed, plus laptops on the desk of every public school student. That enthusiasm is missing in this year’s elections. The lack of a unified Democratic agenda, and the president’s usual reluctance to stay on message, has obscured the trend running under everything. Voters have grown more nervous about their futures and more nostalgic about what they’ve lost. “Even if you are living where your forefathers have lived for generations,” wrote the tech skeptic Paul Kingsnorth last year, “you can bet that the smartphone you gave your child will unmoor them more effectively than any bulldozer could.” Voters want to slow things down. Democrats and Republicans are offering them different ways of doing that. The Trump administration has taken joy in rolling back the renewable energy spending of the Biden administration, stopping wind and solar farms and pushing the auto industry back from its embrace of EVs and greater engine efficiency . Job growth is slower than it was under Biden; they sometimes describe that as cause for celebration, too. “After the deportations that we have seen during President Trump’s administration and the closing of the border… we don’t need to produce as many jobs,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained to CNBC last week. But more voters feel like they’re losing out, and that the industries driving growth right now have made their lives worse — to say nothing of their kids. Where is the techno-optimism? Not in any of the campaigns. The crypto industry has spent tens of millions of dollars to elect a “pro-crypto Congress,” but its ads don’t try to sell voters on the importance of crypto. And ads paid for by the prediction market and gambling industries don’t tout the virtues of those industries. They are, universally , about the issues that voters care about — or that pollsters say they care about. Because those pollsters also find that voters are queasy about the explosion of gambling, and don’t see themselves getting rich by holding onto the right digital coins. Most of the visible voter angst about change is about tech. But some of it is about the cultural change that people argue about, on their phones, with the other angry people that their algorithm has found for them. The recent elite-level Democratic debate about “Woke 1″ was premised on something real. Liberals were embarrassed about the ways they talked about race and gender in 2020, from the pronouns they plunked into their email signatures to the black squares they posted on Instagram. What they were really embarrassed about was their radical, temporary optimism about how that year’s crises would transform the country. The pandemic was going to convince people of the need for universal healthcare; the murder of George Floyd would tear down the carceral state; the end of the Trump administration would reopen the border for millions of asylum-seekers. Democrats now agree that they promised too much change, too quickly, and that Republicans benefited from the backlash. Anti-vaccine activists won the COVID wars; mass deportation advocates came back with more momentum than they’d had in 100 years. Democrats now talk about immigrants as “neighbors” who deserve to stay here, not as more aspiring Americans who should be let in to enrich and transform the country. This is just not a year to tout transformation. The electorate is looking for candidates who’ll protect what they have — jobs, homes, time — and not imperil it in the name of growth or progress. Room for Disagreement One massive exception to this anti-tech mood among Republicans: Industry stocks have surged since Trump took office. Any voter who owns them, individually or in an index fund, is doing better than he was before the new “golden age of America.” Notable In his The Midterms, Actually newsletter, Astead Herndon looked at why both parties were taken by surprise by the data center backlash. “People don’t want to feel like they’re guinea pigs in an experiment, and it’s not just Sam Altman who has contributed to that feeling. It’s also the politicians who have treated technological change as something they retroactively legislate after a crisis arrives.” For Politico, Gabby Miller and Owen Dahlkamp talked to AI industry insiders about the ways they’re responding to political rage. “Now some of Silicon Valley’s biggest dogs are entering the fight.” In his Slow Boring newsletter, Matthew Yglesias shared his own theories on why people aren’t happier about technological progress.

events.title: AI agents may raise conflict-of-interest risks, study finds
events.summary: Does agentic AI have a payola problem? A new Stanford research paper lays out a problem that is being largely ignored as AI takes over internet search and e-commerce: It’s becoming less clear whether recommendations by AI chatbots are driven by advertising dollars or genuine information. In the not-too-distant future, when you want a new toaster, you might just talk to an AI agent about it on your drive home from work, and the next day, your toaster arrives. Behind the scenes, five toaster companies might have bid on what the agent sees. How do you know you really got the best toaster, or the best price? Now extrapolate this problem to weightier areas, like healthcare or financial services and the consequences are pretty serious. If everyone has their own personalized AI agent that’s smart enough to navigate the consumer landscape without falling for misleading marketing, perhaps this becomes a non-issue. But what might be more likely is that the vast majority of people use free chatbots funded by ads. Government regulation might help, with laws that prohibit chatbots from providing advice without disclosing financial incentives. But it might be too opaque to properly police. The time to sort this out is now, before an adtech-like industry springs up around agentic commerce and it becomes too difficult to unravel. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: A former Democratic operative on what the party needs to keep from MAGA
events.summary: The News Not every book by a former “insider” is created equal. “ Nothing Left ” by Evan Barker is unusually rich and well-timed. Barker was a powerhouse fundraiser for the Democratic Party’s left, which meant she was in the room for crucial meetings between its biggest stars, before she got fed up with the movement and voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. Barker dished about her evolution on TikTok, in articles in The Free Press, and then in the book — which, she told me, she wished had come out even sooner. “The first three to four or five months after the election, I think there was a window of opportunity,” she said in an interview from her Bay Area home. “You had Gavin [Newsom] interviewing Steve Bannon and Charlie Kirk. They were willing to talk to the right. It just seemed like there was more openness about debating what needed to change.” When the second Trump administration grew less popular, she worried that the conversation had stopped. “Nothing Left” is a great look behind the curtain at how political fundraising really works, but it also has a thesis: That the “Democrats should take the best parts of MAGA and the best parts of Bernie and marry them,” Barker writes. This is a transcript of a conversation with Barker about the book, which has been lightly edited for length and clarity. The View From Evan Barker David Weigel: There’s a storyline on the left that it’s the 2016 Hillary Clinton campaign that is to blame for injecting identity politics into the party. Where was it actually coming from, the idea that the party should be more culturally progressive? From the center or the left? Evan Barker: They both do it! It’s this weapon that’s sitting in the room and one of them will pick it up and be like: I’m gonna whip out identity politics. There were hints of this with the Brent Welder campaign and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In 2018, you’re working for Welder; he is a white male labor attorney in Kansas City, Kansas. The DCCC wants a Native American candidate who ends up winning. So, what was AOC’s first reaction to the idea of coming out there to campaign for Welder? At first she was amenable, but then there was this mob that formed online. I don’t really know if they were establishment types or what; I wasn’t paying that close of attention to Twitter at that time. But there was this meme of Sharice Davids, who’s now a congresswoman, next to Brent and Bernie, and I think AOC. And it was: Two white men attacked a woman of color. They were @ing AOC and yelling at her. And she wanted to pull out of the event. We got a phone call from her team, and they were just like: Yeah, we’re not sure if she’s gonna still do this. She doesn’t wanna be seen as somebody who’s not supporting a woman of color. Brent responded: No, no, no, it’s not about that. I have the best policies that will help women of color, so that’s why you should come out here and help me. I left this out of the book: Our final donor call was two hours before polls closed. Believe it or not, politicians call donors all the way up until the polls close on election day. She was, like, a max-out ask. And I remember her saying: “I agreed to this call, but I just researched your race. And I found out that you’re running against a woman of color. And I just think it’s terrible that you want to take her place. This is her turn.” That was foreshadowing for what would completely take over the progressive movement. You write that “AOC became a loyal lapdog for the establishment, while the establishment embraced the most divisive aspects of progressive rhetoric.” There’s a debate among centrists who don’t like that this happened; how much did this weaken the Democratic Party? How much did this weaken its institutions? The problem with the centrists is that they are socially to the left, but they’re economically to the right. And that’s just not a pairing that really attracts working class people. That’s not a good match at all. The progressives are socially to the left and economically to the left, which also I think can alienate working class people. The centrists like to just blame the progressives for all of this, but I think it’s unfair: They don’t acknowledge their own issues of not really delivering economic transformation for working class people. At least progressives will talk about those things, although the priorities shifted. I think the ideal faction would be anti-progressive and populist. That’s somebody that’s socially moderate to conservative, but economically left. I don’t think that faction really exists. I’m in that faction. Can you explain what the Race Class Narrative is? For example: “Grocery prices are really expensive right now, but we know that black and brown communities are struggling the most to pay for groceries. So we need to do X, Y, and Z policies to make groceries affordable for all people.” It’s identifying an economic issue and then racializing it, but then saying that you’re gonna do something that will help everybody. Is there anything Trump has done that you want the next president, even if they’re a Democrat, to continue? What do you like, that he’s done? The anti-DEI stuff, absolutely. I think it’s better for everybody if we don’t continue going down that road. Closing the border — obviously, I’m happy about that. Bernie Sanders even said he was happy about that. This might surprise you, but I support the philosophy behind the tariffs. I don’t like the way that they were executed by the administration. What are your thoughts about AOC as the standard bearer of the Bernie movement? Is she well equipped to do that? No, no. I don’t think that she’d be able to win the blue wall. I think she’s really talented, you know? She’s a good speaker. People on the right like to write her off as dumb. She’s not dumb. She’s very smart. But she doesn’t have that broad appeal because she is more focused on identity. And just based on what I know about her and my couple of interactions with her, I don’t think that she is actually going to run for president. I think that she’s too much like — she wants to get along. She wants her colleagues to like her. If Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi showed her polling that said she was not able to win and that it was gonna really hurt the Democratic Party if she ran, I don’t think she would run.

events.title: Exclusive: Waymo says there's no AI shortcut to self-driving
events.summary: Breakthroughs in AI are fueling hopes that more data and smarter models can provide a shortcut to self-driving vehicles. Waymo, after more than 15 years and 200 million driverless miles, says there is none. Why it matters: The answer could determine whether the AV race is a long, expensive slog that rewards Waymo's head start — or a new track that lets newer rivals hit the road faster. Driving the news: Srikanth Thirumalai, Waymo's vice president of onboard software, said in an exclusive interview with Axios that it takes more than just better AI to safely deploy AVs at scale. Waymo's goal from the start, he said, has been "demonstrably safe AI." But a growing reliance from competitors on single "end-to-end" AI systems introduces risks. "Even the best AI models with trillions of parameters still hallucinate... We don't have a choice to say, 'Let's hit refresh' ... There is no click reboot or reload or refresh [in] physical AI. You have to deal with the consequences of it." In a blog post published Wednesday, Thirumalai goes deeper on 10 AI lessons Waymo has gleaned from its first 200 million autonomous miles. Catch up quick: Waymo got its start as Google's self-driving car project in 2009, well before the modern deep-learning revolution. In the early days, it relied on many specialized models — one for pedestrian detection, another to tell when a light turns green, for example. Gradually it shifted toward fewer, larger foundation models, "riding the AI wave," Thirumalai said. Now companies like Tesla, Wayve and Waabi are going even further, developing AV 2.0 systems they say are capable of humanlike reasoning — "end-to-end" neural networks that process raw sensor data and directly output steering commands. Waymo says it has tried the same tools but concluded that there aren't enough safety guardrails. "What we found is that just pure end-to-end systems are not able to meet our safety bar at the scale that we operate," Thirumalai told Axios. Reality check: Thirumalai said Waymo published the blog post to counter a narrative that AI can provide a shortcut to safe self-driving, with public trust in the AV industry on the line. At the same time, it's a flex. The safety standards Waymo wants the industry to embrace — not to mention regulators and rulemakers — also play to its biggest competitive advantage: a big head start built on years of testing and real-world driving data. While it didn't name specific competitors, it laid out reasons why newer approaches to building AV systems could carry risks — effectively raising the bar those companies would have to clear. Zoom in: Waymo weighed in on one of the industry's biggest debates — whether cameras alone can solve full autonomy. When training its models, Waymo found that visibility was far better when cameras, lidar and radar worked together rather than when one or more sensors were eliminated. "The AI can only make sense of what it sees, and if you just can't see it, the AI can't do much," Thirumalai said. Between the lines: It's a direct jab at Tesla, which is betting on a camera-only, end-to-end autonomous driving system. Better AI can't fully compensate for inadequate sensing, Thirumalai said. He added the same is true for high-definition mapping, which some rivals say is unnecessary. The bottom line: Waymo spent more than 15 years building a commanding lead in robotaxis, and Thirumalai argued now that there is no "one silver bullet" to reaching safe autonomy. Waymo's experience as the industry leader gives its argument weight — but it doesn't settle the debate. Rapid advances in AI could still prove there's a faster path to autonomy.

events.title: Trump’s new affordability push runs on highways, rail
events.summary: The Scoop The Trump administration is unveiling a new proposal aimed at turning the nation’s highway and rail lines into “multi-use” utility corridors that could hold critical infrastructure like transmission wires, fiber optic lines, and water pipelines. The plan, dubbed “America’s Great Corridors of Commerce,” is being billed by the Transportation Department as a “voluntary nationwide opportunity,” and comes as the administration looks for ways to drive down energy costs for Americans. The initiative, according to details shared first with Semafor, will allow state-level transportation agencies and railroads to lease out land alongside roads and tracks to private sector companies to develop new infrastructure. “America has always been at the bleeding edge of innovation. But we will lose the race to develop the technologies of the future if we cannot lower costs and get the government out of the way,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement. The new plan, he added, will “make energy more affordable and fuel American industry for generations to come.” The administration hopes that using existing “transportation land” will reduce the cost of projects while leveraging “categorical environmental exemptions to bypass lengthy reviews,” according to a release describing the proposal, which emphasizes the need to quickly build out these types of infrastructure. Know More The Trump administration is also billing the proposal as a way to better compete with China, arguing that the country is ahead of the US in building things like high-voltage transmission lines. One of the biggest obstacles to many new power transmission projects is opposition from local communities and zoning authorities, a problem that can be bypassed if new grid lines stick close to existing infrastructure. In recent months, the administration has ramped up its focus on things like artificial intelligence data centers for similar reasons. The data center debate has increasingly become a focus in the midterms as voters sour on the technology infrastructure. Republican candidates across the are trying to walk the line between appeasing anti-data center voters without straying too far from President Donald Trump’s push for building them. Notably, the new proposal follows the Trump administration’s cancellation of a number of major transmission initiatives. The Energy Department ended a $4.9 billion conditional loan commitment last year for a transmission project and scrapped three other transmission corridor proposals earlier this month. Trump’s focus on leveraging the land — which mirrors proposals that Biden administration officials , environmental groups, and congressional Democrats have advocated for years — offers an alternative to those prior cancelled projects by using highway and railroad-affiliated land. Alan Mitchell, a senior Manager for US federal policy at the Clean Air Task Force, a climate nonprofit, commended the Trump administration’s plan as a “step in the right direction” and a “serious, practical use of existing authority.” But Mitchell argued that the administration’s other actions — like the recent cancellations — could undercut the plan. “The administration needs to act consistently to get our country the transmission it needs where it needs it,” he told Semafor.

events.title: 20pc more children are growing up in rental housing, as ownership rates plunge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More children are growing up in rental housing and moving every couple of years Children whose parents owned the home they lived in had far fewer moves as those who rented. ( ABC News: Curtis Rodda ) A new report by researchers at Adelaide University shows children who grow up in rental housing move every 2.3 years, on average. Around one-in-eight children who grow up in rentals have moved at least 10 times by age 14. The proportion of Australian children growing up in private rental housing jumped by 20 per cent between 2001 and 2023. More children are growing up in private rentals and facing housing insecurity, a new report finds, warning that it could have long-term implications for their development, physical health and mental wellbeing. The study by four researchers at Adelaide University — Amy Clair, Emma Baker, Lynne Giles and Claire Morey — has been released by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute today. By analysing a range of comprehensive and long-term datasets, such as the Household Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey and the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, the authors attempted to determine the effects of Australia's multi-decade housing affordability crisis on children. The report found that as housing prices surged between 2001 and 2023, the proportion of households with children living in homes owned outright plunged 52 per cent. Those in social rentals fell 46 per cent as the public housing sector stagnated, those who owned with a mortgage increased 27 per cent and those in private rentals rose 20 per cent. Australia's true 'home ownership' rate is just over 50pc. Here's why How the census over-inflates the home ownership rate. Research lead and associate professor Amy Clair said the latter statistic was particularly concerning as children growing up in private rental properties moved every 2.3 years on average. "By age 14, a child in a private rental had moved an average of six times. By comparison, those in households that owned their home had moved a little over twice on average, and children in social housing had moved just over four times," she said. The data shows children growing up in households with a mortgage tend to have moved about three times by age 14, which is half as often as those in a family renting. However, those averages also mask more extreme housing instability in many cases. Around one in eight children growing up in private rentals had lived in 10 or more homes by age 14, compared to approximately one in 40 children living in a home owned with a mortgage, the research found. It may not surprise you to learn that few households with children were renting by choice, with only 7 per cent reporting they did so because they preferred it and 8 per cent saying they appreciated its flexibility, while more than half said they did not have a housing deposit saved and around half said they could not afford to buy. AHURI found the most common reasons for renting related to the lack of a deposit to buy a home and other affordability issues. ( Supplied: AHURI ) 'Housing a critical determinant of physical and mental health' The research also showed that children growing up in rental housing were more likely to live in a household suffering financial stress or poor living conditions. Roughly 18 per cent of households with children in private rentals were late on a housing payment, compared to about 7 per cent of households with a mortgage, while around 10 per cent of children in private rentals experienced overcrowding, which was more than twice the rate of children living in owner-occupied homes. Dr Clair said children's experiences were often ignored in the public discussion of housing affordability, partly through a lack of data about their housing status, and better information could help foster the housing conditions that allowed children to thrive. "However, Australia's data is fragmented, creating blind spots that hinder early intervention, response targeting and accountable policy." The report's authors surveyed a wide range of academic literature which generally found links between housing stability and improved developmental outcomes. ( ABC Radio Darwin: Kate O'Toole ) The report suggests that maternal and child health services, early childhood education, schools and primary care services could routinely collect indicators of affordability stress, overcrowding and dwelling problems, while population surveys could include indicators of thermal comfort, damp, mould, crowding, safety and amenity.

events.title: AD Ports board backs L’imad’s Dh6.25-a-share bid for full control
events.summary: AD Ports Group’s board has recommended that shareholders accept L'imad’s Dh6.25-a-share offer to take full control of the Abu Dhabi ports and logistics company, following a fairness opinion from its independent financial adviser HSBC. L'imad, Abu Dhabi’s sovereign investment vehicle, through its wholly owned subsidiary ADQ, launched a voluntary tender offer on August 18 to acquire the remaining shares in AD Ports. ADQ already owns 75.42 per cent of the company. Under the offer, shareholders will receive Dh6.25 ($1.70) in cash for each share they tender. The price represents a 23 per cent premium to AD Ports’ closing price before the bid was announced and is about 95 per cent above the Dh3.20-a-share price at which the company listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange in 2022. The offer values AD Ports at about Dh31.8 billion. Shareholders have until 3pm on September 15 to accept the offer, unless the deadline is extended. Full details of the board’s recommendation and HSBC’s fairness opinion have been published in an AD Ports disclosure to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange. AD Ports appointed HSBC Bank Middle East as its independent financial adviser on August 21 after L'imad announced its intention to acquire the company. L'imad said the offer gives shareholders “an attractive opportunity to realise certain and immediate value”, while allowing AD Ports to pursue long-term growth, including acquisitions, without the constraints of a public listing. The offer is the latest move by L'imad to consolidate strategic assets in Abu Dhabi as it builds a portfolio spanning energy and utilities, ports and logistics, aviation, urban development and industrial sectors. L'imad was set up last year and is expanding its portfolio. In July, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, approved the fund’s investment and operational framework for strategic sectors. This month, L'imad completed its acquisition of the remaining shares in Abu Dhabi National Energy Company, or Taqa, through its subsidiary Abu Dhabi Power Corporation, taking its stake to 100 per cent from 98.12 per cent. Taqa is now awaiting regulatory approval to delist from the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange. L'imad also owns a significant stake in Abu Dhabi real estate developer Modon Holding. AD Ports operates about 40 terminals in the UAE and has a presence in about 50 markets globally.
